title: The divine eye
hook: after a week of hearing, Arjuna asks to see God's real form and is told his eyes won't do; why Hindus go for darshan
carry: darshan: the sight of God is a gift

segments.voice: Yesterday, rasa: I am the taste in water, and every glory a spark. Your line was every glory is a spark of God. Today, the end of the week, and chapter eleven begins.

Ten chapters on a chariot, and Arjuna has heard it all. This week alone: Sudama's rice; chores offered like the milkmaids' churning; the robber who became a poet; the lotus with no bottom; where to look; the taste in water. He believes every word. But hearing about someone you love isn't the same as seeing them. So the warrior turns to his friend and asks for the one thing words can't give.
screen: `TEN CHAPTERS OF HEARING.` → `HEARING ISN'T SEEING.` → `SHOW ME.`

segments.voice: Verse one: out of kindness to me you've told me this highest secret about the self, and my confusion is gone. Verse two: I've heard in detail how beings come and go, and about your greatness that doesn't end. Verse three: it is just as you say. But I want to see it: your form as the Lord of all. Then verse four, a lovely bit of humility: if you think I'm able to see it, master of yoga, show me your imperishable self. If you think I'm able. He doesn't demand. He asks, and leaves room for no. Krishna says yes. Verse five: behold my forms, by hundreds and thousands, divine, of many colors and shapes. Verse six: see the gods of the sky and the storm, wonders no one has seen before. Verse seven: see the whole universe, moving and unmoving, gathered here in my body, and anything else you want to see. Then the catch, verse eight: you can't see me with these eyes of yours, so I give you a divine eye. Divyam chakshuh. Behold my power. That's the key to the whole chapter. Seeing God isn't a matter of looking harder with ordinary eyes; the sight itself has to be given. In the Mahabharata, the narrator Sanjaya, telling all this to the blind king, has been given a divine eye too, so he can see the battlefield from the palace. That's how anyone hearing the story gets to watch. Many Hindus hear the same idea in darshan at the temple: seeing God and being seen, a sight received, not taken.
screen: `MY CONFUSION IS GONE.` · `IF YOU THINK I'M ABLE, SHOW ME.` · `NOT WITH THESE EYES.` · `A DIVINE EYE, GIVEN.` · then, large: `DARSHAN: THE SIGHT IS GIVEN.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and notice that everything you usually look at is gone, yet something is still seeing: shapes, colors, the dark behind the lids. Rest in that. Then think of one thing, or one person, you'd like to see more truly, and without forcing anything, ask in your own way, as Arjuna did: if I'm able, show me.
Divyam chakshuh. A divine eye. After hearing, Arjuna asks for sight, and Krishna gives him this eye, because ordinary eyes can't see it.
Your line: darshan, the sight of God is a gift. Arjuna asked, and left room for no. A whole week, done.

howItsDone: Many Hindus speak of darshan, seeing and being seen by the divine, when they visit a temple; chapter eleven, where Arjuna asks to see and is given a divine eye, is often read as the Gita's great darshan.
